ONCOLOGICAL EMERGENCIES IN THE ED 
 
 
ONCOLOGICAL EMERGENCIES 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
LOCAL EFFECTS 
• SVC syndrome 
• Malignant pericardial effusion 
• Malignant spinal cord compression 
• Brain metastases 
 
BIOCHEMICAL EFFECTS 
• Tumour Lysis Syndrome 
• Hypercalcaemia 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Diagnosing any oncological emergency requires a high index of suspicion 
Patient might be known with a malignancy or may be undiagnosed 
 
HAEMATOLOGICAL EFFECTS 
• Neutropenic fever 
• Hyperviscosity syndrome 
• VTE

MALIGNANT PERICARDIAL EFFUSION 
• Cancers: Lung, breast, oesophageal, melanoma, leukaemia, lymphoma 
• Life-threatening = tamponade 
• Can have rapid (more dangerous) vs chronic accumulation 
• Signs and Symptoms 
■ Exertional dyspnoea, chest pain, tachycardia, pulsus paradox 
■ Beck’s triad: Muffled heart sounds, distended neck veins, 
hypotension (only 1/3 patients) 
■ Worrying signs: Tachypnoea, tachycardia, hypotension, narrow 
pulse pressure, altered GCS 
• Bedside U/S 
■ Fluid around heart 
■ Danger signs: RA collapse in late diastole, RV collapse in early 
diastole 
• ECG: Low amplitude QRS, electrical alternans 
• CXR: Increased cardiac shadow (increased cardio-thoracic ratio) 
• Emergent Rx: Pericardiocentesis (Emergency ED procedure in tamponade) 
■ U/S guided - Seldinger technique with CVP set 
➔ NB! DO NOT SLASH MYOCARDIUM 
■ Elevate bed 30-45, aseptic, identify deepest pocket of fluid 
parasternal/apical/subxiphoid view, insert needle above rib with 
U/S guidance into pericardial sac 
• Supportive treatment 
■ Fluid resus only if hypovolaemic 
■ Try avoiding intubation - worsens haemodynamic status 
• Disposition 
■ Oncology referral if known patient (by inpt dept)
ONCOLOGICAL EMERGENCIES 
LOCAL EFFECTS 
 
SVC SYNDROME 
• Mechanical obstruction SVC 
Internal: Clot 
External: Tumour/Lymph node 
• Cancers: Lung, NH Lymphoma 
• Sx depends on extent obstruction and rapidity of onset 
• Signs and symptoms 
Dyspnoea, facial oedema, cough, chest pain, dysphagia, 
distended neck veins, facial plethora, arm oedema 
RARE and DANGEROUS vocal cord oedema 
• CXR: Can be normal, widened mediastinum, pleural effusion 
• CT gold standard 
• Treatment 
Manage airway if needed (NB! expect difficult airway) 
Elevate head, supportive treatment 
Steroids: Dexamethasone 8mg STAT 
Consider anti-coagulation (if thrombus suspected) 
• Disposition 
Oncology referral by inpt dept 
Ultimate Rx: Chemotherapy, radiotherapy, stenting

MALIGNANT SPINAL CORD COMPRESSION 
• Cancers: Breast, prostate, lung, lymphoma, MM 
• Symptoms vary according to level of compression 
• Signs and Symptoms 
Back pain (especially if worsens at night/when lying) 
Bladder/bowel Sx, lower limb weakness, sensory deficit 
(NB! saddle anaesthesia), acute paralysis 
• Imaging: 
X-Rays: Can lack sensitivity 
CT 
Best = MRI 
• Treatment 
Supportive care 
Pain management 
Neurology: Dexamethasone 10mg STAT 
• Disposition 
Urgent Ortho Spine referral 
Urgent Radiation oncology referral (by inpt dept) 
 
BRAIN METASTASIS 
• Most common oncological neurological manifestation 
• Cancer: Melanoma, lung, breast, liver, thyroid 
• Increase ICP (Mass, vasogenic oedema, acute haemorrhage) 
• Signs and Symptoms 
Headache, focal signs 
As ICP: N+V, seizures, decreased GCS 
• Imaging 
Contrast CT Brain 
• Treatment 
Supportive care, head up 
Steroids: Dexamethasone 8mg STAT 
Anti-convulsant if presenting with seizures 
Impending herniation: can consider osmotic diuresis 
(hypertonic saline) 
• Disposition 
Neurosurgery/Neurology referral 
Oncology referral (if known oncology patient, by inpt dept) 
Ultimate Rx: Radiotherapy +/- surgery 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
References 
1. EMDocs. Oncological Emergencies Part I: Pearls and Pitfalls. Available: http://www.emdocs.net/oncologic-emergencies-part-i-pearls-and-pitfalls/ [accessed 18/08/2020] 
2. EMDocs. Oncological Emergencies Part II: Pearls and Pitfalls. Available: http://www.emdocs.net/oncologic-emergencies-part-ii-pearls-and-pitfalls/ [accessed 18/08/2020] 
3. Dubbs SB. Akilesh PH. 2018. Rapid fire: Central Nervous System Emergencies. Emerg Med Clin N Am. 36(3); 537-548. 
4. Umar AK. Shanholtz CB. McCurdy MT. 2014. Oncologic Mechanical Emergencies. Emerg Med Clin N Am. 32(3); 495-508. 
ONCOLOGICAL EMERGENCIES 
LOCAL EFFECTS

TUMOUR LYSIS SYNDROME 
• Metabolic emergency = massive tumour cell lysis 
■ Release tumour cell contents into circulation 
■ Electrolyte derangement: Ca2+ K+ PO4 Uric Acid 
■ Renal failure, metabolic acidosis, seizures, cardiac 
arrythmias 
• Trigger 
■ Chemotherapy, radiotherapy, high dose steroids, 
hormonal therapy, surgery, rapidly growing tumour 
• Risk 
■ Leukaemia, lymphoma, aggressive Rx, high tumour 
burden 
• Signs and symptoms 
■ GIT upset, lethargy, decreased urine output, cramps, 
cardiac arrythmias, delirium, seizures 
• Diagnostic criteria: Cairo-Bishop ➔ 
• Treatment 
■ Monitored bed 
■ Aggressive IV fluids (Balanced crystalloid) 
➔ Aim for urine output > 2ml/kg/hr 
■ If volume overloaded: Lasix® 
■ Manage electrolyte abnormalities 
■ Supportive treatment 
■ Dialysis indications ➔ oliguria, anuria, volume overload, 
persistent hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia-induced 
symptomatic hypocalcaemia 
• Disposition 
■ Urgent Oncology referral by inpt dept 
■ ICU referral for severe cases 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
References 
1. EMDocs. Oncological Emergencies Part I: Pearls and Pitfalls. Available: http://www.emdocs.net/oncologic-

2. EMDocs. Oncological Emergencies Part II: Pearls and Pitfalls. Available: http://www.emdocs.net/oncologic-

3. Wagner J. Arora S. 2014. Oncologic Metabolic Emergencies. Emerg Med Clin N Am. 32(3); 509-525 
ONCOLOGICAL EMERGENCIES 
BIOCHEMICAL 
 
HYPERCALCAEMIA 
Stones, Bones, Abdominal Moans and Psychic Groans 
• Most common causes: Hyperparathyroidism and malignancies 
• Nearly all cancers 
• Most common: MM, breast, lung, kidney 
• Symptoms 
Neuro: Fatigue, muscle weakness, hyporeflexia, 
delirium, low GCS 
GIT: N+V, constipation, ileus, PUD, pancreatitis 
Cardiac: Arrythmias 
Renal: Polydipsia, polyuria, kidney stones, AKI 
General: Pruritis, dehydration 
• ECG: Osborne waves, ST elevation, shortened QTc, 
widened T-wave, bundle branch type patterns, heart 
block, brady-dysrhythmias 
• Treatment 
Monitored bed 
Aggressive IV fluids 
If overloaded: Consider Lasix® bolus 
Bisphosphates (Prolonged onset action) 
• Disposition 
Oncology referral if known, by inpt dept 
Renal referral if unknown

NEUTROPENIC FEVER 
• Fever + neutropaenia: consider life-threatening infection 
Trigger: Rapid work-up and empiric AB 
• Neutropaenia: Absolute neutrophil count <1000/microlitre 
Many causes (e.g. Malignancy, chemotherapy, HIV, 
other medications) 
Often 5-10 days after last chemotherapy dose 
• Fever (Can be only Sx: High clinical suspicion) 
Single oral temp > 38.3°C or > 38°C for > 1 hour 
• (See Protocol - Sepsis and Septic Shock in the ED) 
• Look carefully for signs of infection but defer PR (typhlitis) 
Look everywhere including skin, mucous 
membranes, peri-anal, indwelling lines/catheters 
Consider typhlitis: Necrotising enterocolitis, 
!appendicitis mimic! CT Abdo, NGT, NPO, IV Fluid 
• Send appropriate samples 
• Early AB, consider Fungal cover 
Consider likely organism, broad cover/nosocomial 
cover 
Tazocin adequate broad spectrum 
• Differential Dx: Drug reaction, PE, other onc emergency 
• Disposition 
Early oncology referral by inpt dept 
 
HYPERVISCOSITY SYNDROME 
• Increased serum viscosity 
Elevated proteins/cellular constituents (WCC) 
Microvascular complications, sluggish blood flow 
and impaired platelet function 
• MM, acute leukaemia 
• High clinical suspicion 
• Signs and symptoms 
Triad: Mucosal/skin bleeds, visual disturbances, 
neuro Sx 
Dyspnoea, hypoxia, end organ dysfunction, 
fever, MI, cardiac failure, acute limb, delirium, 
stoke 
• Treatment 
Supportive 
Fluid resus 
• Ultimate Rx: lower WCC/protein 
chemo/plasmapheresis 
• Disposition 
Urgent Oncology referral by inpt dept 
VTE 
See VTE protocol
